title: MICROPLASTIC IN MANGROVE SEDIMENTS: IMPLICATIONS FOR SUSTAINABLE COASTAL MANAGEMENT

MICROPLASTIC IN MANGROVE SEDIMENTS: IMPLICATIONS FOR SUSTAINABLE COASTAL MANAGEMENT

ABSTRACT

Mangrove ecosystems trap plastic debris, leading to longer plastic waste residence time, which promotes the formation of microplastic and accumulation in sediment. Microplastic impairs the growth of mangrove and adversely affects other organisms within the ecosystem, which may lead to increased benthic and plankton mortality. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the morphology and the abundance of microplastic in mangrove ecosystems of Sabang City and to understand the interaction between sampling location, fraction, and the type of microplastic in the two different depths of the sediment. The coastal area was sampled in the four mangrove ecosystems, namely Balohan, Jaboi, Gapang, and Iboih. The results showed that the four morphotypes identified in the sediment were film, fiber, fragment, and pellets, with the most abundant being fiber. The highest overall abundance occurred at the subsurface depths of 20–40 cm, while the maximum abundances of fiber, film, fragment, and pellet were 2340, 1600, 920, and 60 particles/kg, respectively, across all sampling stations. Visual characterization showed a diverse range of colors that included transparent, blue, red, yellowish brown, and black. Overall, microplastic contamination was found in 100% of mangrove sediments sample locations at the study area. There were a significant relationship between the sediment fraction with the type and abundance microplastic. In summary, these results emphasize that mangrove sediments are significant traps and the ecological hazards caused in coastal ecosystems and benthic communities should be highlighted.
